phy_edx.1.0.summary: Physical quantities are either **scalars**, which have **magnitude (size) only**, or **vectors**, which have **both magnitude and direction**. Edexcel expects you to explain this difference and recall the standard pairs: distance and displacement, speed and velocity, mass and weight, plus acceleration, force, momentum and energy. The key idea for motion is that **velocity is speed in a stated direction**, so an object can travel at a constant speed while its velocity changes, and average speed is found from distance travelled divided by time taken.

core.h: Scalars and vectors: the core difference
core.p: Every physical quantity is either a scalar or a vector. The difference is whether **direction** matters. A scalar is fully described by a number and a unit. A vector also needs a direction, because the same size of quantity acting in different directions has different effects.
bullets: **Scalar**: magnitude only, for example a mass of 5 kg.
**Vector**: magnitude and direction, for example a force of 5 N to the left.
Magnitude means the size of the quantity, always given with a unit.
Direction can be given as left/right, up/down, north/south, an angle, or a positive or negative sign.
Two vectors are only equal if both their sizes and their directions are the same.

callouts.p: A quantity that has magnitude (size) only.
A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction.

core.p: The specification lists the quantities you must be able to classify. Learn them in pairs, because many exam questions ask you to name the vector that matches a given scalar.
bullets: Distance (scalar) and **displacement** (vector).
Speed (scalar) and **velocity** (vector).
Mass (scalar) and **weight** (vector, because it is a force acting downwards).
**Acceleration** is a vector.
**Force** is a vector.
**Momentum** is a vector (it has the direction of the velocity).
**Energy** is a scalar; time is also a scalar.

callouts.p: Displacement, velocity, acceleration, force, weight and momentum are vectors. Distance, speed, mass and energy are scalars.

core.p: A vector is drawn as an **arrow**. The **length** of the arrow represents the magnitude (drawn to scale) and the **arrowhead** shows the direction. This is how forces are shown on free body diagrams.
bullets: A longer arrow means a larger magnitude.
Arrows must be drawn to a stated scale, for example 1 cm = 10 N.
The arrow points in the direction of the quantity.
In one dimension, one direction is chosen as positive and the opposite direction is negative.
A scalar cannot be drawn as an arrow because it has no direction.

core.p: **Distance** is how far an object travels along its actual path, whatever direction it goes. **Displacement** is the straight-line distance from the start point to the finish point, **in a stated direction**. They are only equal when an object moves in a straight line without turning back.
bullets: Distance is a scalar; displacement is a vector.
Walking 3 m east then 3 m west: distance = 6 m, displacement = 0 m.
Running one full lap of a 400 m track: distance = 400 m, displacement = 0 m (back at the start).
Displacement can be smaller than distance but never larger.
Both are measured in metres (m).

callouts.p: The distance moved in a straight line from the starting point in a stated direction.

core.p: **Speed** is the distance travelled per unit time. It tells you how fast something is moving but not which way. Speed is a scalar, measured in metres per second (m/s).
bullets: (average) speed = distance / time, or v = x / t.
distance travelled = average speed x time.
time = distance / average speed.
Speed in m/s means the number of metres travelled each second.
A speedometer shows **instantaneous speed**; a journey calculation gives **average speed**.

callouts.p: (average) speed (m/s) = distance (m) / time (s), and distance travelled (m) = average speed (m/s) x time (s). These are not given on the equation sheet, so learn them.

core.p: Real objects rarely move at a constant speed: cars speed up at junctions and slow down at traffic lights. **Average speed** is the total distance divided by the total time for the whole journey. **Instantaneous speed** is the speed at one particular moment.
bullets: Average speed smooths out all the speeding up and slowing down.
Average speed = total distance / total time, including any time spent stopped.
Instantaneous speed is what a speed camera or speedometer measures.
A car could have an average speed of 30 km/h on a journey but reach 50 km/h at some points.

callouts.p: For a journey in two parts, you cannot just add the two speeds and divide by 2. Find total distance and total time first.

core.p: **Velocity is speed in a stated direction.** It is a vector, measured in m/s, and you must always say which way the object is moving. Two cars moving at 20 m/s in opposite directions have the same speed but different velocities.
bullets: Velocity = displacement / time.
Example: 15 m/s north, or -15 m/s if north is taken as positive and the car moves south.
A change in **speed** or a change in **direction** (or both) is a change in velocity.
The magnitude of velocity is the speed.
A negative velocity does not mean slow; it means moving in the opposite direction to the one chosen as positive.

callouts.p: Velocity is speed in a stated direction.

core.p: Because velocity includes direction, an object moving at a **steady speed** around a curve or circle has a **changing velocity**. Its direction is always changing, so its velocity is always changing, even though its speed stays the same.
bullets: A car going round a roundabout at a steady 10 m/s has a changing velocity.
A satellite in a circular orbit moves at constant speed but changing velocity.
At any instant the velocity points along the tangent to the circle.
A change in velocity means the object is accelerating, so a resultant force must act (this links to circular motion and Newton's laws).

callouts.p: Constant speed in a circle is still acceleration, because acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, and velocity is changing direction.

core.h: Why mass is a scalar but weight is a vector
core.p: **Mass** is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kilograms. It has no direction, so it is a scalar. **Weight** is the gravitational force acting on that mass, measured in newtons, and it always acts **towards the centre of the Earth** (downwards), so it is a vector.
bullets: Mass: scalar, kg, the same everywhere.
Weight: vector, N, depends on gravitational field strength.
Because weight is a force, and all forces are vectors, weight must be a vector.
In everyday language people say 'I weigh 60 kg', but in physics that is a mass.

callouts.p: Never give weight in kilograms. Weight is a force, so its unit is the newton.

core.h: Force, acceleration and momentum as vectors
core.p: Forces, accelerations and momenta all have direction, which is why they are vectors. Direction matters because it decides the effect: a force pushing forwards speeds a car up, the same force pushing backwards slows it down.
bullets: **Force**: a push or pull with a direction, measured in N.
**Acceleration**: rate of change of velocity, in m/s^2; it points in the direction of the change in velocity.
A negative acceleration (deceleration) means acceleration in the opposite direction to the motion.
**Momentum** = mass x velocity; since velocity is a vector and mass is a scalar, momentum is a vector in the direction of the velocity.
**Energy** is a scalar: kinetic energy is the same whichever way an object moves.

callouts.p: A scalar multiplied by a vector gives a vector (mass x velocity = momentum). If a quantity is built from velocity or displacement, it is usually a vector.

core.h: Adding vectors in a straight line
core.p: When vectors act along the same line, you add them taking direction into account. Choose one direction as positive. Vectors in that direction are positive, vectors in the opposite direction are negative. Scalars simply add.
bullets: Forces of 8 N right and 5 N left give a resultant of 3 N to the right.
Velocities of a walker at 1.5 m/s on a moving walkway at 1.0 m/s in the same direction give 2.5 m/s relative to the ground.
Walking 1.5 m/s against a 1.0 m/s walkway gives 0.5 m/s in the walker's direction.
Masses of 2 kg and 3 kg always add to 5 kg, because mass is a scalar.

callouts.p: When you give a vector answer, include the direction: '3 N to the right', not just '3 N'.

core.p: Edexcel expects you to have a sense of everyday speeds, which helps with estimates and checking whether answers are sensible.
bullets: Walking: about 1.5 m/s.
Running: about 3 m/s.
Cycling: about 6 m/s.
Car in town: about 13 m/s; on a motorway about 30 m/s.
Speed of sound in air: about 330 m/s.
These values vary, so exam answers in a sensible range are accepted.

analogy.t: Scalars and vectors are like directions to a friend's house
analogy.p: Telling a friend 'my house is 2 km away' is like giving a scalar: they know how far but could walk 2 km in any direction and never find you. Saying '2 km north' is a vector: size and direction together get them to the right place. Distance is the route they actually walk; displacement is the 'as the crow flies' arrow from their door to yours. The analogy breaks down because real directions often involve several turns, and some vectors (like force or acceleration) are not about places at all.

exam.q: State the difference between a scalar quantity and a vector quantity.
model: a vector has magnitude and direction
exam.tip: Use the word magnitude or size in both halves of the answer.

exam.q: Which of these is a vector quantity? A energy B mass C speed D momentum
exam.tip: Momentum = mass x velocity, so it has direction.

exam.q: Which of these is a scalar quantity? A acceleration B distance C force D weight
exam.tip: All forces, including weight, are vectors.

exam.q: Name the vector quantity that corresponds to speed.
exam.tip: Learn the scalar/vector pairs.

exam.q: State what is meant by velocity.
exam.tip: This is a word-for-word definition; learn it exactly.

exam.q: A student walks 120 m in 80 s. Calculate her average speed.
exam.tip: The speed equation is not on the equation sheet, so you must recall it.

exam.q: A car travels at an average speed of 25 m/s for 3 minutes. Calculate the distance travelled.
exam.tip: Convert minutes to seconds before substituting.

exam.q: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m circular track. Explain why the distance travelled and the displacement are different.
model: distance is 400 m, the length of the path travelled
displacement is 0 m because the runner finishes at the start point
exam.tip: Give the values as well as the reasons.

exam.q: A satellite orbits the Earth at a constant speed. Explain why its velocity is not constant.
model: velocity is speed in a given direction / velocity is a vector
the direction of motion is continuously changing
exam.tip: Mention direction explicitly; that is the scoring idea.

exam.q: A train travels 30 km in 20 minutes, stops for 10 minutes, then travels 45 km in 30 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s for the whole journey.
exam.tip: The stop counts as part of the total time.

exam.q: Explain the difference between mass and weight and why one is a scalar and the other a vector.
model: mass is the amount of matter in an object, measured in kg
mass has magnitude only so it is a scalar
weight is the gravitational force on the mass, measured in N
weight acts in a direction (towards the centre of the Earth / downwards) so it is a vector
exam.tip: Give units and directions for full marks.

worked.q: A cyclist rides 3.6 km in 10 minutes. Calculate her average speed in m/s.
A boat travels 800 m east and then 200 m west in a total time of 250 s. Find (a) the distance travelled, (b) the displacement, (c) the average speed and (d) the average velocity.
steps: (b) take east as positive: displacement = +800 - 200 = +600 m, so 600 m east
(d) average velocity = displacement / time = 600 / 250 = 2.4 m/s east

worked.q: Classify each quantity as scalar or vector and explain: 50 kg, 490 N downwards, 1500 J, 12 m/s north.
steps: 50 kg is a mass: magnitude only, so scalar
490 N downwards is a weight (a force): magnitude and direction, so vector
1500 J is energy: magnitude only, so scalar
12 m/s north is a velocity: speed with a stated direction, so vector

phy_edx.1.1.summary: Speed tells you how much distance an object covers in each second, and Edexcel wants you to **recall and use** the equation **distance travelled = average speed × time** (x = v × t) with distances in metres, times in seconds and speeds in m/s. A distance-time graph is a picture of a journey: a flat line means the object is stationary, a straight sloping line means a **constant speed**, and a curve means the speed is changing. The key skill is that the **gradient of a distance-time graph equals the speed**, so a steeper line means a faster object and you can calculate the speed by dividing the change in distance by the change in time.

core.h: Distance, time and speed: the basic quantities
core.p: Before using any equation you need to know exactly what each quantity means and which unit it is measured in. Edexcel uses the SI units of metres, seconds and metres per second, and mark schemes often give a separate mark for the correct unit.
bullets: **Distance** is how far an object travels along its path, measured in **metres (m)**. It is a **scalar**: it has size (magnitude) only.
**Time** is measured in **seconds (s)**. Convert minutes and hours to seconds before calculating: 1 min = 60 s, 1 h = 3600 s.
**Speed** is the distance travelled per unit time, measured in **metres per second (m/s)**. It is also a scalar.
In the Edexcel equation sheet style, distance is given the symbol **x**, speed **v** and time **t**.
Speed only tells you how fast; it does not tell you the direction. Velocity (covered in 2.1-2.5) is speed in a stated direction.
Other speed units you may meet: km/h, mph and cm/s. Exams usually want answers in m/s unless the question says otherwise.

callouts.p: Speed is the distance travelled per unit time (per second).

core.p: This is a **recall and use** equation, so it will NOT be given to you on the equation sheet: you must learn it word for word. It links the distance travelled to how fast the object goes on average and for how long it travels.
bullets: **distance travelled (m) = average speed (m/s) × time (s)**
In symbols: **x = v × t**
Rearranged for speed: **average speed = distance travelled ÷ time**
Rearranged for time: **time = distance travelled ÷ average speed**
WHY it works: if you cover 5 m every second, then in 10 seconds you cover 10 lots of 5 m = 50 m.
Always write the equation first, then substitute numbers, then give the answer with a unit: this gains method marks even if your final answer is wrong.
Use the formula triangle (distance on top, speed and time on the bottom) if rearranging is hard for you, but practise rearranging algebraically too.

callouts.p: distance travelled = average speed × time. This equation is not on the Edexcel equation sheet.

core.p: Real objects rarely travel at exactly the same speed the whole time. Cars slow down at junctions and speed up again, runners start slowly and sprint at the end. That is why the spec equation uses **average speed**.
bullets: **Average speed = total distance travelled ÷ total time taken** for the whole journey.
**Instantaneous speed** is the speed at one particular moment, for example the reading on a car speedometer.
An object can have an average speed of 10 m/s and yet at some moments be stationary and at others travel at 20 m/s.
For a multi-stage journey you must add up ALL the distances and ALL the times, including any time spent stationary, before dividing.
Do NOT simply average the speeds of each stage unless every stage lasts the same time: the stages usually last different times.
If an object moves at a constant speed, its average speed and instantaneous speed are the same at every moment.

callouts.p: When a question asks for average speed for the whole journey, the time spent stopped is still part of the total time.

core.p: Many marks are lost not on the physics but on the units. Convert everything into metres and seconds BEFORE you put numbers into the equation, then the answer comes out in m/s automatically.
bullets: km to m: multiply by 1000 (2.4 km = 2400 m).
cm to m: divide by 100 (35 cm = 0.35 m).
minutes to seconds: multiply by 60 (4 min = 240 s).
hours to seconds: multiply by 3600 (0.5 h = 1800 s).
km/h to m/s: divide by 3.6 (72 km/h = 20 m/s). WHY: 1 km/h = 1000 m ÷ 3600 s.
m/s to km/h: multiply by 3.6.
Give answers to a sensible number of significant figures, usually the same as the data in the question (2 or 3 s.f.).
Use standard form for very large distances, for example light travelling 3.0 × 10^8 m in one second.

callouts.p: A person walking at 140 m/s or a car at 0.2 m/s means a unit conversion has gone wrong. Walking is about 1.5 m/s and a car in town is about 13 m/s.

core.p: A distance-time graph plots **distance travelled on the y-axis** against **time on the x-axis**. Reading it is like replaying the journey: each point tells you how far the object has gone at that moment.
bullets: **Horizontal (flat) line**: the distance is not changing, so the object is **stationary** (speed = 0).
**Straight sloping line**: equal distances are covered in equal times, so the object moves at a **constant speed**.
**Steeper straight line**: more distance per second, so a **higher constant speed**.
**Curve getting steeper**: the speed is increasing, so the object is **accelerating**.
**Curve getting less steep (flattening)**: the speed is decreasing, so the object is **decelerating**.
On a true distance-time graph the line can never slope downwards, because distance travelled never decreases.
You can read off how far the object has travelled at any time, or the time at which it has travelled a given distance.

callouts.p: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph means stationary, NOT constant speed. On a velocity-time graph a horizontal line means constant velocity: do not mix the two up.

core.h: Gradient of a distance-time graph = speed
core.p: The **gradient** (steepness) of a distance-time graph is the change in distance divided by the change in time. That is exactly how speed is defined, so **gradient = speed**. This is the central idea of spec 2.7.
bullets: **gradient = change in distance (y-axis) ÷ change in time (x-axis)**, often written as rise ÷ run.
Step 1: pick two points on the straight line that are far apart (a big triangle reduces reading errors).
Step 2: draw a right-angled triangle under the line between them.
Step 3: read the change in distance (vertical side) and change in time (horizontal side) using the axis scales, not by counting squares unless each square has a known value.
Step 4: divide: speed = change in distance ÷ change in time. Unit is m/s if the axes are in m and s.
A straight line has the same gradient everywhere, so the speed is constant and any two points on the line give the same answer.
Comparing gradients: the steeper line has the larger gradient and therefore the higher speed.

callouts.p: Examiners want to see the triangle drawn on the graph and the values read from the scale. A large triangle earns the method mark and gives a more accurate answer.

core.h: Interpreting the shape of the graph
core.p: Exam questions often show a graph and ask you to describe the motion in each section. Use the precise words in the table: examiners reward **stationary**, **constant speed**, **accelerating** and **decelerating**, and they also reward comparisons such as 'faster than in section A'.
bullets: Describe each section in order and quote values: 'from 0 to 20 s it travels 100 m at a constant speed of 5 m/s'.
When comparing two sections, say which is steeper AND therefore which speed is higher.
If a straight line becomes steeper at a corner, the speed has suddenly increased (a sharp corner is an idealisation; real changes take time).
A line through the origin means the object started at zero distance at time zero.
The total distance travelled is the final y-value; the total time is the final x-value.

callouts.p: For 'describe the motion' questions, a top answer names the motion for each section and calculates the speed using the gradient where the line is straight.

core.p: When the line is curved the speed is changing, so there is no single gradient. To find the **instantaneous speed** at one moment, Higher tier students draw a **tangent** to the curve at that point and find the gradient of the tangent.
bullets: A **tangent** is a straight line that just touches the curve at one point and has the same steepness as the curve there.
Draw it with a ruler, making the angle between tangent and curve look equal on both sides of the point.
Make the tangent long, then use a large triangle on the tangent to find change in distance ÷ change in time.
The gradient of the tangent = the speed at that instant.
A curve that gets steeper shows **acceleration**; a curve that levels off shows **deceleration**.
The **average speed** over a curved section is still total distance ÷ total time (the gradient of a straight line joining the start and end points), which is different from the instantaneous speed.

callouts.t: Do not use a single point
callouts.p: Dividing the distance at one point by its time (y ÷ x) gives the average speed from the start, not the instantaneous speed. For speed at an instant you need the tangent's gradient.

core.p: A graph question may ask for the average speed over the whole journey even when the object stops or changes speed. Use the end points, not the individual sections.
bullets: Read the **total distance** from the last point on the y-axis.
Read the **total time** from the last point on the x-axis.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
This average is lower than the fastest section and higher than the slowest section.
If the object stops for part of the journey, the stopped time is included, so the average is pulled down.
Graphically, the average speed is the gradient of a straight line joined from the start point to the end point.

callouts.p: Total distance ÷ total time is the same as the gradient of the straight line joining the start and end of the journey.

core.p: Some questions show a graph where the line comes back down to zero, for example a person walking to a shop and back home. Strictly this is a **displacement-time** graph (distance from the starting point), not a distance travelled graph.
bullets: Distance travelled always increases or stays the same, so a distance-time graph never slopes down.
On a displacement-time graph a downward slope means moving back towards the start.
The gradient of a displacement-time graph gives **velocity**; a negative gradient means moving in the opposite direction.
For a round trip, the total distance travelled is the sum of the outward and return distances, but the final displacement may be zero.
Read the axis label carefully: 'distance from home' behaves like displacement.

callouts.p: A person walking 300 m to a shop and 300 m back has travelled 600 m, even though they end where they started.

core.h: Plotting a distance-time graph from data
core.p: You may be given a table of distances and times (for example from a trolley experiment) and asked to plot the graph. Good graph technique earns easy marks.
bullets: Put time (the independent variable) on the x-axis and distance on the y-axis.
Label both axes with the quantity and unit, for example 'distance / m' and 'time / s'.
Choose a linear scale that uses more than half of the grid.
Plot points accurately with small neat crosses.
Draw a single straight line of best fit with a ruler, or a smooth curve if the points clearly curve. Do not join dot to dot.
Then use a large triangle on the line of best fit to find the gradient (speed).

callouts.p: Use the line of best fit, not the individual data points, when working out the gradient: the line averages out random errors.

core.h: Linking ideas: why gradient means speed
core.p: Grade 9 answers explain the reasoning, not just the rule. The gradient is the rate of change of the y-axis quantity with time, and speed is the rate of change of distance with time.
bullets: Gradient = vertical change ÷ horizontal change = change in distance ÷ change in time.
Speed = distance travelled ÷ time taken. These are the same calculation, so gradient = speed.
If the speed is constant, distance increases by the same amount each second, giving a straight line.
If the speed increases, distance increases by more each second, so the line curves upwards (gets steeper).
This same idea extends to velocity-time graphs, where the gradient is acceleration (spec 2.10).

callouts.p: The gradient of any graph against time tells you how fast the y-axis quantity is changing.

analogy.t: A distance-time graph is a journey diary
analogy.p: Imagine a diary where every second you write down how far you have walked in total. If you write the same number again and again, you were standing still (flat line). If the number goes up by the same amount every entry, you are walking steadily (straight slope), and the bigger the jump each time, the faster you are walking (steeper slope). It breaks down because a diary only has separate entries, whereas a real graph is continuous, and the diary never tells you which direction you walked in, just like speed and distance, which are scalars.

terms.d: How far an object travels along its path; a scalar measured in metres (m).
The distance travelled per unit time; a scalar measured in metres per second (m/s).
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken for the journey.
The speed of an object at one particular moment in time.
Moving the same distance in every equal interval of time; shown by a straight sloping line on a distance-time graph.
Not moving; speed is zero; shown by a horizontal line on a distance-time graph.
A graph of distance travelled (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for a journey.
The steepness of a line: change in y-value divided by change in x-value.
A straight line that touches a curve at one point and has the same gradient as the curve at that point.
Speeding up; shown by a distance-time curve that gets steeper.
Slowing down; shown by a distance-time curve that gets less steep.
A quantity with magnitude (size) only and no direction, such as distance, speed and time.
The distance from the starting point in a stated direction; a vector quantity.
The SI unit of speed: one metre travelled every second.

mistakes.w: A horizontal line on a distance-time graph shows constant speed.
mistakes.r: A horizontal line shows the object is stationary (speed = 0); constant speed is a straight sloping line.

mistakes.w: speed = time ÷ distance
mistakes.r: average speed = distance travelled ÷ time taken.

mistakes.w: Using minutes or km directly, for example 3 km ÷ 2 min = 1.5 m/s.
mistakes.r: Convert to metres and seconds first: 3000 m ÷ 120 s = 25 m/s.

mistakes.w: Average speed of a journey = (speed 1 + speed 2) ÷ 2.
mistakes.r: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, including any time stationary.

mistakes.w: Finding speed by counting squares without using the scale.
mistakes.r: Read the change in distance and change in time from the axis scales and divide.

mistakes.w: Reading y ÷ x at a single point on a curve to get the speed at that moment.
mistakes.r: Draw a tangent at that point and calculate its gradient (Higher).

mistakes.w: The steeper line shows the object travelling further.
mistakes.r: The steeper line shows a greater speed (more distance per second), not necessarily a greater total distance.

mistakes.w: Leaving out the time stopped when calculating average speed for the whole journey.
mistakes.r: The total time includes the time spent stationary.

mistakes.w: Writing the answer without a unit, or with m/s² for speed.
mistakes.r: Speed is in m/s.

exam.q: State the equation linking distance travelled, average speed and time.
model: distance travelled = average speed × time (or any correct rearrangement)
exam.tip: Words or standard symbols are accepted; this equation is not given on the sheet.

exam.q: A train travels 4.5 km in 3 minutes. Calculate its average speed in m/s.
exam.tip: Convert to m and s before substituting; a correct answer with the unit gains full marks.

exam.q: A cyclist rides at an average speed of 6.0 m/s for 25 minutes. Calculate the distance travelled.
exam.tip: Watch the time conversion: 25 min is 1500 s.

exam.q: How long does it take a sound wave travelling at 340 m/s to travel 1020 m?
exam.tip: Rearrange the equation before substituting.

exam.q: What does a horizontal line on a distance-time graph show?
model: the object is stationary / not moving / speed is zero
exam.tip: Constant speed would get no marks.

exam.q: Explain how a distance-time graph can be used to find the speed of an object moving at constant speed.
model: find the gradient of the line
by dividing the change in distance by the change in time (using a triangle)
exam.tip: Mention both 'gradient' and how to calculate it.

exam.q: A distance-time graph for a runner shows a straight line from (0 s, 0 m) to (40 s, 200 m), a horizontal line to 60 s, then a straight line to (100 s, 400 m). Calculate the runner's speed in the first and last sections.
exam.tip: Use the change in distance and change in time for each section, not the final readings.

exam.q: For the runner in the previous question, calculate the average speed for the whole 100 s.
exam.tip: The average is lower than 5 m/s because the 20 s rest is included.

exam.q: The distance-time graph for a car is a curve that becomes steeper. Describe the motion of the car and explain how you could find its speed at t = 5 s.
model: the car is accelerating / its speed is increasing
draw a tangent to the curve at t = 5 s
speed = gradient of tangent = change in distance ÷ change in time
exam.tip: Higher tier: the word 'tangent' is a marking point.

exam.q: Describe in detail the motion shown by a distance-time graph that has four sections: a straight slope from 0 to 10 s reaching 50 m, a horizontal line from 10 s to 20 s, a steeper straight slope reaching 150 m at 30 s, and a curve that levels off reaching 180 m at 50 s. Include calculations.
model: 20-30 s: constant speed, faster than first section
30-50 s: decelerating / slowing down as gradient decreases (to stop, average 1.5 m/s)
exam.tip: Six-mark answers need every section named and quantified where the line is straight; compare sections.

worked.q: A car travels 1.2 km along a road in 1 minute 20 seconds. Calculate its average speed.
steps: Write the equation: average speed = distance travelled ÷ time

worked.q: A walker covers 400 m in 300 s, stops for 120 s to rest, then covers 600 m in 180 s. Calculate the average speed for the whole journey.
steps: average speed = total distance ÷ total time

worked.q: On a distance-time graph, a straight line passes through (2 s, 10 m) and (8 s, 40 m). Find the speed of the object and the distance it travels in 30 s at this speed.

phy_edx.1.2.summary: Acceleration is the **rate of change of velocity**: how much the velocity changes every second. Edexcel requires you to **recall and use** a = (v - u) ÷ t, and to **use** the equation v² - u² = 2 × a × x (given on the equation sheet), which links velocities, acceleration and distance without needing the time. Both equations apply to **uniform (constant) acceleration**, use velocities in m/s, time in s, distance in m and acceleration in **m/s²**, and a negative acceleration means the object is slowing down (deceleration).

core.p: Acceleration tells you how quickly the velocity is changing. An object accelerates whenever its velocity changes: speeding up, slowing down, or changing direction. At GCSE most calculations are for objects moving in a straight line.
bullets: **Acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken**.
An acceleration of 3 m/s² means the velocity increases by **3 m/s every second**.
Acceleration is a **vector**: it has size and direction, because velocity is a vector.
**Speeding up**: acceleration in the same direction as the velocity (positive).
**Slowing down (deceleration)**: acceleration opposite to the velocity (negative value in calculations).
Changing direction at constant speed (for example circular motion) is also acceleration, because the velocity changes; that idea is developed in 2.20-2.21.
Zero acceleration means constant velocity: the velocity does not change at all.

callouts.p: Acceleration is the change in velocity per unit time (the rate of change of velocity).

core.p: This is a **recall and use** equation: you must learn it, because it is not on the equation sheet. It comes straight from the definition: change in velocity is final velocity minus initial velocity.
bullets: **acceleration (m/s²) = change in velocity (m/s) ÷ time taken (s)**
In symbols: **a = (v - u) ÷ t**
**u** = initial velocity (at the start), **v** = final velocity (at the end), **t** = time taken for the change.
Change in velocity = v - u. Always final minus initial, so a slowing object gives a negative answer.
Rearranged: **v - u = a × t**, so **v = u + a × t**, and **t = (v - u) ÷ a**.
'Starts from rest' or 'stationary' means u = 0 m/s. 'Comes to a stop' means v = 0 m/s.
The equation gives the **average acceleration** over the time; if acceleration is uniform this is the acceleration at every instant.

callouts.p: a = (v - u) ÷ t is a recall equation. v² - u² = 2 × a × x is given on the equation sheet, but you must be able to select and use it.

core.p: Students often find the 'squared' in the unit strange. It comes straight from dividing a velocity by a time.
bullets: Acceleration = velocity ÷ time = (m/s) ÷ s = **m/s²** (metres per second per second).
Read 4 m/s² as '4 metres per second, every second': velocity grows by 4 m/s each second.
It is NOT the same as m/s (speed) or m (distance); using the wrong unit loses the unit mark.
Sometimes written m s^-2; this means the same thing.
If time is given in minutes or velocity in km/h, convert to s and m/s first.

callouts.p: Writing m/s for acceleration is one of the most common lost marks. Acceleration is always m/s².

core.p: When an object slows down, its final velocity is smaller than its initial velocity, so v - u is negative and the acceleration comes out negative. A negative acceleration in the direction of motion is called a **deceleration**.
bullets: Example: a car slows from 20 m/s to 5 m/s in 5 s: a = (5 - 20) ÷ 5 = -3 m/s².
You can say 'acceleration = -3 m/s²' or 'deceleration = 3 m/s²', but not 'deceleration = -3 m/s²' (double negative).
A deceleration acts in the opposite direction to the velocity: when braking, the acceleration points backwards.
When using v² - u² = 2 × a × x for a braking object, put a in as a **negative** number.
Large decelerations (for example in crashes) are dangerous; that is developed in 2.31.

callouts.p: Choose the direction of motion as positive. Anything slowing the object down then has a negative acceleration.

core.h: Using a = (v - u) ÷ t step by step
core.p: Follow the same method every time and you will collect every method mark. Write down what you know first, then the equation, then substitute.
bullets: 1. List the values: u = ?, v = ?, t = ?, a = ? (with units).
2. Convert units to m/s and s.
3. Write the equation: a = (v - u) ÷ t.
4. Rearrange if needed before substituting (for example v = u + at).
5. Substitute and calculate; do the subtraction v - u first.
6. Give the answer with unit m/s² (or m/s, or s, depending on what you found) and a sensible number of significant figures.
Check: does a speeding-up object have a positive a, and a slowing one a negative a?

callouts.p: Write (24 - 0) ÷ 8 rather than jumping to 3. The substitution line is usually worth a mark on its own.

core.h: The equation v² - u² = 2 × a × x (spec 2.9)
core.p: This equation links initial velocity, final velocity, acceleration and distance, **without the time**. It is given on the Edexcel equation sheet, but you must know when to choose it and how to rearrange it.
bullets: **(final velocity)² - (initial velocity)² = 2 × acceleration × distance**
In symbols: **v² - u² = 2 × a × x**, where x is the distance travelled (m).
Use it when the question gives or asks for a **distance** and does **not** mention time.
It only works for **uniform (constant) acceleration** in a straight line.
Rearranged for v: **v² = u² + 2ax**, then v = square root of (u² + 2ax).
Rearranged for a: **a = (v² - u²) ÷ (2x)**.
Rearranged for x: **x = (v² - u²) ÷ (2a)**.
Square the velocities BEFORE subtracting: v² - u² is not the same as (v - u)².

callouts.t: Do not forget to square root
callouts.p: When finding a velocity you get v² first. Many students stop there; the final step is to take the square root.

core.p: Both equations have u, v and a. The deciding question is whether the problem involves **time** or **distance**.
bullets: Time given or asked for: use **a = (v - u) ÷ t**.
Distance given or asked for, no time: use **v² - u² = 2 × a × x**.
Sometimes you need both: for example find a from the distance, then use a to find the time.
List the known quantities as u, v, a, x, t and cross out the one not involved.
For falling objects near the Earth's surface, the acceleration is about **10 m/s²** (g ≈ 9.8 m/s²; the value of g is covered more fully in 2.13).
If an object is dropped, u = 0; if thrown upwards and reaching the top, v = 0 at the top.

callouts.p: No t in the question? Reach for v² - u² = 2ax.

core.h: Where v² - u² = 2ax comes from (for understanding)
core.p: You do not need to derive it, but understanding it helps you trust it. It combines the acceleration equation with the idea that, for uniform acceleration, the average velocity is halfway between u and v.
bullets: Average velocity for uniform acceleration = (u + v) ÷ 2.
Distance = average velocity × time, so x = (u + v) ÷ 2 × t.
From a = (v - u) ÷ t, the time is t = (v - u) ÷ a.
Substitute: x = (u + v)(v - u) ÷ 2a = (v² - u²) ÷ 2a.
Multiply both sides by 2a: v² - u² = 2ax.
This shows why it needs uniform acceleration: the 'average = halfway' step is only true then.

callouts.p: Both v² - u² = 2ax and using (u + v) ÷ 2 as the average velocity require constant acceleration.

core.h: Velocity squared: why doubling speed matters so much
core.p: Because velocity is squared, distance does not grow in simple proportion to speed. This links forward to braking distances in 2.28-2.33.
bullets: Starting from rest, v² = 2ax, so for the same acceleration x is proportional to v².
Doubling the final velocity needs **four times** the distance (2² = 4).
Tripling the velocity needs nine times the distance.
For a braking car with the same deceleration, doubling the initial speed makes the braking distance four times longer.
This is why small increases in speed make a big difference to safety.

callouts.p: If asked how distance changes when speed doubles, answer 'it quadruples (× 4) because x is proportional to v²'.

core.p: Acceleration can also be found from a graph. On a velocity-time graph the gradient equals the acceleration; the full method is spec 2.10, but the link to the equation is worth knowing.
bullets: The y-axis shows velocity, so the rise of the line is v - u.
The x-axis shows time, so the run of the line is t.
Gradient = rise ÷ run = (v - u) ÷ t = a.
A steeper line means a larger acceleration; a downward slope means deceleration.
A straight line means uniform acceleration, which is when both equations in this point are valid.

callouts.p: a = (v - u) ÷ t is exactly the gradient of a velocity-time graph.

core.p: Edexcel sets these equations in everyday situations. Recognising the context helps you spot which values are zero.
bullets: **Car accelerating from traffic lights**: u = 0.
**Car braking to a stop**: v = 0, a negative.
**Object dropped from a height**: u = 0, a ≈ 10 m/s² (downwards).
**Ball thrown straight up**: at the top v = 0; a = -10 m/s² if up is positive.
**Aircraft on a runway**: often find the runway length x needed using v² - u² = 2ax.
**Sprinter**: find the acceleration over the first few seconds using a = (v - u) ÷ t.

callouts.p: Underline phrases like 'from rest', 'dropped', 'comes to a stop': each tells you a velocity is zero.

analogy.t: Acceleration is like your savings rate
analogy.p: Think of velocity as the money in a savings account and acceleration as how much you add each week. Adding £4 every week is like an acceleration of 4 m/s² (velocity grows by 4 m/s every second); taking money out each week is a deceleration. The balance (velocity) can be large while the weekly change (acceleration) is zero, just as a car can be fast but not accelerating. It breaks down because money has no direction, whereas velocity and acceleration are vectors, and the v² in the second equation has no simple money equivalent.

exam.q: State the unit of acceleration.
exam.tip: m/s will not score.

exam.q: Write down the equation that links acceleration, change in velocity and time taken.
model: acceleration = change in velocity ÷ time taken (a = (v - u) ÷ t)
exam.tip: This is a recall equation, so you must know it.

exam.q: A car accelerates from rest to 24 m/s in 8.0 s. Calculate its acceleration.
exam.tip: 'From rest' tells you u = 0.

exam.q: A cyclist slows from 12 m/s to 4 m/s in 4.0 s. Calculate the acceleration and explain the sign of your answer.
model: negative because the cyclist is slowing down / decelerating
exam.tip: Final minus initial gives the sign automatically.

exam.q: A sprinter accelerates at 2.5 m/s² for 3.2 s from rest. Calculate her final velocity.
model: v = u + a × t (rearranging a = (v - u) ÷ t)
exam.tip: Rearrange before substituting.

exam.q: A stone is dropped from rest and falls 45 m. The acceleration is 10 m/s². Calculate its velocity just before it hits the ground.
exam.tip: No time is mentioned, so choose v² - u² = 2ax; remember the square root.

exam.q: An aircraft must reach 80 m/s to take off. It accelerates uniformly from rest at 2.0 m/s². Calculate the minimum length of runway needed.
exam.tip: Rearrange for x and keep the 2 in the denominator.

exam.tip: Enter the deceleration as -6.0 m/s² in both equations.

phy_edx.1.3.summary: A velocity-time graph shows how an object's velocity changes over time, and Edexcel spec 2.10 asks you to analyse it in three ways. You must **compare accelerations qualitatively from the gradients** (steeper means greater acceleration), **calculate the acceleration from the gradient** for uniform acceleration, and **find the distance travelled from the area between the line and the time axis** for uniform acceleration. Reading the graph correctly depends on remembering that a flat line here means constant velocity, not stationary, which is the opposite of a distance-time graph.

core.p: A velocity-time graph has **velocity on the y-axis** (m/s) and **time on the x-axis** (s). Each point tells you how fast, and in which direction, the object is moving at that moment.
bullets: The y-value at any time is the **instantaneous velocity**.
A point on the time axis (velocity = 0) means the object is **stationary** at that instant.
Velocity is a vector, so values below the time axis would mean moving in the opposite direction; most GCSE graphs stay above the axis.
Two key features to analyse: the **gradient** (gives acceleration) and the **area under the line** (gives distance travelled).
Always check the axis labels: a velocity-time graph and a distance-time graph can look the same but mean completely different things.

callouts.p: Gradient of a velocity-time graph = acceleration. Area between the line and the time axis = distance travelled.

core.p: The shape of each section tells you the type of motion before you do any calculation. Use the precise terms examiners reward.
bullets: **Horizontal line above the axis**: constant velocity, acceleration = 0.
**Horizontal line on the time axis**: stationary (v = 0).
**Straight line sloping upwards**: **uniform (constant) acceleration**.
**Straight line sloping downwards**: **uniform deceleration** (negative acceleration).
**Steeper straight line**: greater acceleration (or greater deceleration if sloping down).
**Curve getting steeper**: acceleration increasing; **curve levelling off**: acceleration decreasing, for example a falling object approaching terminal velocity.

callouts.p: On a velocity-time graph a horizontal line means constant velocity, NOT stationary. Only a line along the time axis (v = 0) means stationary.

core.p: Spec 2.10(a) asks you to compare accelerations by looking at gradients, without calculating. The steeper the line, the faster the velocity is changing, so the greater the acceleration.
bullets: Steeper upward slope = **greater acceleration**.
Gentler upward slope = **smaller acceleration**.
Steeper downward slope = **greater deceleration**.
Horizontal line = **zero acceleration** (constant velocity).
A curve whose gradient decreases shows the acceleration getting smaller; the object is still speeding up, just more slowly.
When comparing, use comparative words and give the reason: 'section A has a greater acceleration than section C because its gradient is steeper'.

callouts.p: Statements like 'A accelerates more' only get full marks when linked to 'because the gradient is steeper'.

core.p: Spec 2.10(b): for a straight-line section (uniform acceleration), **acceleration = gradient = change in velocity ÷ time taken**. This is the same as a = (v - u) ÷ t from spec 2.8.
bullets: Step 1: choose two points on the straight section, as far apart as possible.
Step 2: draw a right-angled triangle under the line.
Step 3: read the change in velocity (vertical side) from the y-axis scale.
Step 4: read the change in time (horizontal side) from the x-axis scale.
Step 5: acceleration = change in velocity ÷ change in time, in **m/s²**.
A downward-sloping section gives a negative gradient: a negative acceleration (deceleration).
Edexcel only asks you to calculate acceleration from a gradient for **uniform acceleration** (straight sections).

callouts.p: The gradient of a velocity-time graph is equal to the acceleration of the object.

core.p: Grade 9 answers explain the link. The gradient of any graph against time is the rate of change of the y-axis quantity.
bullets: Gradient = rise ÷ run = change in velocity ÷ change in time.
Acceleration is defined as change in velocity ÷ time taken.
These are the same calculation, so gradient = acceleration.
Compare: on a distance-time graph, gradient = speed, because the y-axis there is distance.
A straight line has the same gradient everywhere, so the acceleration is uniform.

callouts.p: The gradient tells you how quickly the y-axis quantity changes each second.

core.h: Distance travelled from the area under the graph
core.p: Spec 2.10(c): the **area between the graph line and the time axis** equals the **distance travelled**. For uniform acceleration the shapes are rectangles, triangles or trapeziums, so the area can be calculated exactly.
bullets: Rectangle (constant velocity): area = velocity × time, which is just distance = speed × time.
Triangle (uniform acceleration from rest or to rest): area = ½ × base × height = ½ × time × change in velocity.
Trapezium (uniform acceleration from u to v): area = ½ × (u + v) × t, or split into a rectangle plus a triangle.
Split complicated graphs into simple shapes, find each area, then **add them**.
Use the axis scale values, not the number of centimetres on the page.
Units: (m/s) × s = **m**, so the area gives a distance in metres.
Edexcel asks for this calculation only for uniform acceleration (straight-line sections).

callouts.p: The area between the line and the time axis of a velocity-time graph is equal to the distance travelled.

core.p: Understanding this means you will never forget it. For a short time interval, distance = velocity × time, which is the area of a thin strip under the line.
bullets: At constant velocity, distance = velocity × time = height × width of the rectangle under the line.
When velocity changes, imagine slicing the area into very thin strips; each strip's area is velocity × a tiny time = a tiny distance.
Adding all the strips gives the total area, which is the total distance.
For uniform acceleration, the area of the trapezium equals average velocity × time, because the average velocity is (u + v) ÷ 2.
This is the same reasoning used to derive v² - u² = 2ax (spec 2.9).

callouts.p: For uniform acceleration, distance = ½ × (u + v) × t, which is the trapezium area.

core.h: Average velocity from a velocity-time graph
core.p: Once you have the total distance from the area, you can find the average speed for the journey.
bullets: Average speed = total distance (total area) ÷ total time.
For a single uniformly accelerating section, the average velocity = (u + v) ÷ 2.
For a whole journey with several stages, do NOT average the velocities: find the total area first.
The average lies between the minimum and maximum velocities on the graph.

callouts.p: Edexcel often asks 'calculate the distance travelled' then 'calculate the average speed': the second part uses your answer to the first.

core.p: Many marks are lost by treating one type of graph as the other. Always read the y-axis label before answering.
bullets: Distance-time: gradient = speed; flat line = stationary.
Velocity-time: gradient = acceleration; flat line = constant velocity; area = distance.
A straight upward line on a distance-time graph is constant speed, but on a velocity-time graph it is constant acceleration.
There is no useful 'area' on a distance-time graph at GCSE.

callouts.p: Before describing any graph, say to yourself which quantity is on the y-axis.

core.p: A reliable routine prevents careless errors in multi-part questions.
bullets: 1. Read the axes, including units and the value of each small square.
2. Split the graph into sections at every corner.
3. For each section, name the motion (accelerating, constant velocity, decelerating).
4. For acceleration: gradient of the straight section, with a sign.
5. For distance: area of each section, then add.
6. Show your working on the graph (triangles, shaded areas) and in writing.
7. Give units: m/s² for acceleration, m for distance.

callouts.p: Drawing the triangle or shading the area on the graph helps the examiner award method marks.

core.p: The last section of many journeys slopes down to the time axis as the object stops. Both rules still apply.
bullets: The gradient is negative, so the acceleration is negative (a deceleration).
Example: velocity falls from 20 m/s to 0 in 5 s: gradient = (0 - 20) ÷ 5 = -4 m/s².
The area under this section is a triangle: ½ × 5 × 20 = 50 m, the distance travelled while slowing down.
Distance is still positive: area above the time axis always counts as distance travelled.
In a car this area represents the braking distance (linked to 2.28-2.30).

callouts.p: A downward slope does not make the area negative. The object is still moving forwards while it slows down.

analogy.t: A velocity-time graph is like a tap filling a bath
analogy.p: Imagine the y-axis is how fast water flows from a tap (litres per second) and the x-axis is time. The total water in the bath is flow rate × time, which is the area under the graph, just as distance is the area under a velocity-time graph. How quickly you turn the tap up or down is like the gradient, which is the acceleration. It breaks down because water flow has no direction, whereas velocity is a vector, and a bath cannot 'un-fill' itself by the flow going negative in the same way an object can reverse direction.

terms.d: A graph of velocity (y-axis) against time (x-axis) for a moving object.
The steepness of a line: change in y-value divided by change in x-value.
The rate of change of velocity, equal to the gradient of a velocity-time graph; unit m/s².
Constant acceleration; shown by a straight sloping line on a velocity-time graph.
Slowing down; shown by a line sloping downwards towards the time axis (negative gradient).
Velocity that does not change; shown by a horizontal line above the time axis; zero acceleration.
Not moving; shown by the line lying on the time axis (velocity = 0).
The area between the velocity-time line and the time axis, equal to the distance travelled.
How far the object has moved along its path, in metres.
A four-sided shape with one pair of parallel sides; its area is ½ × (sum of parallel sides) × width.
(u + v) ÷ 2, the velocity halfway between initial and final velocities.
The velocity at the start of the section, read where the section begins.
The velocity at the end of the section, read where the section ends.
Comparing without calculating, for example saying one gradient is steeper so its acceleration is greater.

mistakes.w: A horizontal line on a velocity-time graph means the object is stationary.
mistakes.r: A horizontal line means constant velocity (zero acceleration); stationary is a line on the time axis.

mistakes.w: The gradient of a velocity-time graph gives the speed.
mistakes.r: The gradient gives the acceleration.

mistakes.w: Distance = final velocity × total time for an accelerating object.
mistakes.r: Distance = area under the graph, for example ½ × base × height for a triangle.

mistakes.w: Forgetting the ½ in the area of a triangle.
mistakes.r: Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height.

mistakes.w: Reading the velocity at one point and dividing by its time to get acceleration when the object did not start from rest.
mistakes.r: Use change in velocity ÷ change in time for the section.

mistakes.w: Giving the acceleration unit as m/s or the distance unit as m/s.
mistakes.r: Acceleration in m/s², distance in m.

mistakes.w: Counting centimetres or squares without applying the scale.
mistakes.r: Use the axis values to find the real velocity and time.

mistakes.w: Treating the area of a decelerating section as negative and subtracting it.
mistakes.r: The area above the time axis is distance travelled and is added.

mistakes.w: Saying 'it accelerates more' without a reason.
mistakes.r: Say it has a greater acceleration because the gradient is steeper.

exam.q: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
exam.tip: Not speed: that is the gradient of a distance-time graph.

exam.q: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
exam.tip: Say 'distance travelled' in full.

exam.q: Describe the motion shown by a horizontal line above the time axis on a velocity-time graph.
exam.tip: 'Stationary' scores zero.

exam.q: Two sections of a velocity-time graph, P and Q, both slope upwards. P is steeper than Q. Compare the accelerations in P and Q.
model: acceleration in P is greater than in Q
because P has a steeper gradient
exam.tip: Comparison plus reason.

exam.q: A velocity-time graph is a straight line from 4 m/s at 1 s to 16 m/s at 4 s. Calculate the acceleration.
model: gradient = change in velocity ÷ change in time
exam.tip: Use changes, not the final readings.

exam.q: A car decelerates uniformly from 20 m/s to rest in 5.0 s. Using a velocity-time graph, calculate the distance it travels while stopping.
exam.tip: Sketching the triangle helps.

exam.q: A train accelerates uniformly from 10 m/s to 30 m/s in 20 s. Calculate the distance travelled in this time.
model: area of trapezium = ½ × (u + v) × t
exam.tip: Or rectangle (10 × 20 = 200 m) plus triangle (½ × 20 × 20 = 200 m).

exam.q: A cyclist accelerates uniformly from rest to 8 m/s in 4 s, then travels at 8 m/s for 10 s. Calculate the total distance travelled and the average speed.
exam.tip: Add the areas, then divide by the total time.

exam.q: Explain why the area under a velocity-time graph is equal to the distance travelled.
exam.tip: Link the units: m/s × s = m.

exam.q: A velocity-time graph for a lift shows: uniform acceleration from 0 to 2.0 m/s in 2 s, constant velocity of 2.0 m/s for 6 s, uniform deceleration to rest in 4 s. Describe the motion and calculate the acceleration in each stage and the total distance travelled.
exam.tip: Structure the answer stage by stage, with motion, gradient and area for each.

worked.q: A velocity-time graph shows a straight line from 0 m/s at 0 s to 20 m/s at 5 s. Calculate the acceleration and the distance travelled.
steps: Acceleration = gradient = change in velocity ÷ change in time
Distance = area under the line, a triangle

worked.q: A bus accelerates uniformly from rest to 12 m/s in 6 s, travels at 12 m/s for 10 s, then decelerates uniformly to rest in 4 s. Calculate the total distance and the deceleration.
steps: Stage 3 gradient = (0 - 12) ÷ 4 = -3 m/s², a deceleration of 3 m/s²

worked.q: On a velocity-time graph, a runner's velocity increases uniformly from 3 m/s to 7 m/s between t = 2 s and t = 10 s. Find the acceleration and the distance covered in this time.

phy_edx.1.4.summary: Spec points 2.11 to 2.13 are about measuring speed in the laboratory, knowing realistic everyday speeds and accelerations, and free fall. You need to describe methods such as **light gates**, a **metre rule and stopwatch**, a ticker timer and video analysis, and say why automatic timing is more accurate than human timing. You must recall typical speeds for walking, running, cycling, cars, trains, wind and sound, recall that the **acceleration in free fall, g, is about 10 m/s²**, and use these values to estimate the size of everyday speeds and accelerations.

core.h: Speed is found from distance and time
core.p: Every laboratory method for finding speed comes down to measuring two things: a **distance** and the **time** taken to travel it. The equation is the same one from 2.6: average speed = distance travelled / time taken (v = x / t). What changes from method to method is how precisely the distance and, especially, the time are measured.
bullets: Distance is measured in **metres (m)** using a metre rule, tape measure, trundle wheel or by a known length such as a card on a trolley.
Time is measured in **seconds (s)** using a stopwatch, a light gate and timer or data logger, a ticker timer or the frame rate of a video.
Speed is in **m/s**. Convert cm to m (divide by 100) and ms to s (divide by 1000) before you calculate.
Most methods give the **average speed** over the measured distance. To get something close to the **instantaneous speed**, the distance (or time) measured must be very short.
The shorter the time interval, the bigger the effect of a timing error, which is why short times must be measured automatically.

callouts.p: speed (m/s) = distance (m) / time (s). Rearranged: distance = speed x time, time = distance / speed.

core.h: Method 1: metre rule (or tape measure) and stopwatch
core.p: The simplest method is to mark out a known distance, then time how long the object takes to cover it with a stopwatch. It works well for slow, long journeys such as a person walking 20 m across a field, but is poor for short, fast events because of **human reaction time**.
bullets: Measure and mark a start line and finish line a known distance apart with a **tape measure** or **trundle wheel** (for long distances) or a **metre rule** (for short ones).
Start the stopwatch as the object passes the start line and stop it as it passes the finish line.
Calculate speed = distance / time.
Human **reaction time** is about **0.2 to 0.3 s**, and it affects both starting and stopping the watch. This causes a **random error** (and possibly a systematic one if the timer always reacts late).
Reduce the effect by using a **longer distance** (so the time is longer and the reaction-time error is a smaller fraction of it), and by **repeating** and calculating a **mean**.
Have the timer stand at the finish line and start on a clear signal so they are not judging two distant events.

callouts.p: A 0.2 s error in a 2 s time is 10 percent. The same 0.2 s error in a 20 s time is only 1 percent. Longer times make the reaction-time error relatively smaller.

core.h: Method 2: a single light gate and a card
core.p: A **light gate** sends a beam of light (often infrared) from one side to a detector on the other. When an object breaks the beam, a connected **timer or data logger** records how long the beam is blocked. If a card of known length is fixed to a trolley, the speed as it passes through the gate is the card length divided by the time the beam was blocked.
bullets: Measure the **length of the card** (in the direction of motion) with a ruler and convert to metres.
Fix the card upright on the trolley so it, and only it, cuts through the beam.
Let the trolley pass through the gate. The data logger records the time the beam is **interrupted**.
speed = length of card / time beam is blocked.
Because the card is short (often 5 to 10 cm) the time is very short, so this gives close to the **instantaneous speed** at the gate.
Light gates remove **human reaction time** and can record times to about a thousandth of a second, so they are **more accurate** and **more precise** than a stopwatch.
Many data loggers calculate and display the speed automatically if you type in the card length.

callouts.p: A device that detects when an object passes through it by the object interrupting a beam of light; it is connected to a timer or data logger that measures the time the beam is blocked.
Use the length of the part that actually blocks the beam. If the whole trolley breaks the beam, use the trolley length.

core.h: Method 3: two light gates to find acceleration
core.p: With **two light gates** a set distance apart, the data logger finds the speed at each gate and the time taken to travel between them. From these it can calculate **acceleration**, which links this spec point to 2.8 (a = change in velocity / time) and 2.9 (v² - u² = 2ax).
bullets: Gate A gives the initial speed u = card length / time blocked at A.
Gate B gives the final speed v = card length / time blocked at B.
The logger also records the **time between the gates**, t.
acceleration a = (v - u) / t.
Alternatively, measure the **distance x between the gates** with a metre rule and use v² - u² = 2ax, so a = (v² - u²) / 2x.
A **double interrupt card** (a card with a gap in it) through a single gate gives two speeds and the time between them, so one gate can also measure acceleration.
This set-up is used in the core practical on force, mass and acceleration (2.19).

callouts.p: In a 'describe a method' answer say exactly what is measured (card length, time at each gate, time between gates) and which equation is used.

core.h: Method 4: ticker timer, motion sensor and video analysis
core.p: Other laboratory methods also replace human timing with a reliable clock. Each records position at known time intervals so you can work out distance per unit time.
bullets: **Ticker timer**: a strip of paper tape attached to the trolley is pulled through a timer that makes **50 dots per second**, so the time between dots is **0.02 s**. Measure the distance between dots: dots spread further apart mean higher speed; increasing spacing means acceleration.

**Ultrasound (or other) motion sensor**: sends out pulses and times the echoes to find the distance to the object many times a second; the data logger plots distance-time or velocity-time graphs directly.
**Video analysis**: film the moving object next to a metre rule. The camera records a known number of **frames per second**, so counting frames gives the time and the scale gives the distance.
**Speed cameras and radar** used on roads work on the same principle: a known distance and an automatically measured time.
All these methods give many readings quickly, reduce human error and allow graphs of motion to be drawn.

callouts.p: 50 dots per second, so each dot interval = 1 / 50 = 0.02 s. Ten intervals = 0.2 s.

core.p: Exam questions often ask you to evaluate a method or suggest an improvement. The key ideas are **accuracy** (how close to the true value), **precision/resolution** of the timer, and how much **human error** is involved.
bullets: Stopwatch methods suffer from **reaction time**, which is large compared with short times.
Light gates and data loggers measure time **automatically** and to a much higher resolution (about 0.001 s).
Repeat readings and calculate a **mean** to reduce the effect of **random errors**.
Check that the distance is measured correctly (for example, from the same point on the object each time) to avoid **systematic errors**.
For a very fast object over a short distance, only automatic timing is suitable.

Measures
Main advantage

rows: No reaction time, close to instantaneous speed
Speeds at two points and time between
Gives acceleration as well as speed
Gates must be aligned with card
Needs scale in view or clear echo

callouts.p: 'Use light gates instead of a stopwatch' earns credit only with the reason: 'to remove human reaction time' or 'times are measured more accurately'.

core.h: Typical everyday speeds you must recall
core.p: Edexcel expects you to know realistic speeds so you can make estimates and spot silly answers. These are typical values, so the exam accepts a sensible range, but the values below are the ones most textbooks and mark schemes use.
bullets: **Walking**: about **1.5 m/s**.
**Running**: about **3 m/s** (a sprinter can reach about 10 m/s).
**Cycling**: about **6 m/s**.
**Car in a town (built-up area)**: about **13 m/s** (30 mph).
**Car on a motorway**: about **31 m/s** (70 mph).
**Train**: up to about **50 m/s** for fast trains.
**Passenger aircraft (cruising)**: about **250 m/s**.
**Wind**: a breeze is a few m/s; a strong wind is about 10 to 20 m/s; storm winds are above 20 m/s.
**Sound in air**: about **330 to 340 m/s**.
**Light** (for contrast): 300 000 000 m/s, so light from an event arrives effectively instantly compared with sound.

callouts.p: Walk 1.5, run 3, cycle 6, sound 330 to 340 m/s. These come up most often.

core.p: A 'typical' speed is not fixed. The speed at which a person walks, runs or cycles depends on several factors, and exam questions may ask you to name some.
bullets: **Age** and **fitness** of the person.
**Terrain** (uphill, downhill, rough ground) and surface.
**Distance travelled**: people cannot sustain a sprint, so average speed falls over long distances.
**Weather**, especially wind direction and strength.
For vehicles: **speed limits**, traffic and road conditions.
The speed of sound depends on the **medium** and on temperature; it is much faster in liquids and solids than in air.

callouts.t: Speed of sound is not a speed of a 'thing'
callouts.p: Sound is a wave; 330 to 340 m/s is the speed at which the vibration travels through air, not the speed of air particles moving across the room.

core.h: Using typical speeds to make estimates
core.p: Because you know typical speeds, you can estimate distances or times without being given the speed. Show the value you assumed, then use distance = speed x time.
bullets: Walking to school for 20 minutes: 1.5 m/s x 1200 s = 1800 m, about **2 km**.
Cycling for 10 minutes: 6 m/s x 600 s = 3600 m, about **4 km**.
Thunder heard 3 s after lightning: distance = 340 x 3 = about **1000 m**, because light arrives almost instantly.
An echo from a cliff 170 m away returns after about 2 x 170 / 340 = **1 s** (sound travels there and back).
Always convert minutes and hours to **seconds** first.
Round sensibly: an estimate should usually be given to 1 or 2 significant figures.

callouts.p: Write 'assume walking speed = 1.5 m/s' before calculating. Many estimation mark schemes give a mark for a sensible assumed value.

core.h: Free fall and the acceleration g
core.p: An object is in **free fall** when the **only force acting on it is its weight** (gravity). Near the Earth's surface every object in free fall accelerates downwards at the same rate, whatever its mass. Edexcel wants you to recall that this **acceleration in free fall, g, is 10 m/s²** (more precisely 9.8 m/s²).
bullets: **10 m/s²** means the velocity of a falling object **increases by 10 m/s every second**.
Dropped from rest: after 1 s it moves at 10 m/s, after 2 s at 20 m/s, after 3 s at 30 m/s (ignoring air resistance).
The distance fallen each second gets bigger because the object is going faster, so the gaps in a strobe photo increase.
Heavy and light objects fall with the **same acceleration** in free fall; a feather and a hammer land together on the Moon or in a vacuum.
In air, **air resistance** acts upwards and increases with speed, so real objects accelerate less than g and eventually reach **terminal velocity**.
The same number, 10 N/kg, is the gravitational field strength used in W = m x g (2.16 to 2.18).

callouts.p: Motion of an object when the only force acting on it is its weight (gravitational force), so it accelerates at g, about 10 m/s², near the Earth's surface.
g = 10 m/s² (acceleration in free fall). Use 10 unless the question gives 9.8 or 9.81.
